body_md:
Assign O as $-2$ (no peroxide, no fluorine). Let the oxidation state of Cr be $x$.

$2x + 7(-2) = -2$, so $2x = +12$ and $x = +6$.

Each Cr is $+6$, the same as in chromate, $\ce{CrO4^2-}$.

distractor_notes.A: +3 is Cr in $\ce{Cr^3+}$ or $\ce{Cr2O3}$; it does not balance the charge here.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: $2x - 14 = -2$ gives $x = +6$.
distractor_notes.C: +7 comes from forgetting the $2-$ charge on the ion ($2x - 14 = 0$).
distractor_notes.D: +12 is the total for both Cr atoms, not the oxidation state of one.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Half-reactions:

Reduction: $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O}$

Oxidation: $\ce{Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+ + e-}$ (×5)

Sum: $\ce{MnO4- + 5Fe^2+ + 8H+ -> Mn^2+ + 5Fe^3+ + 4H2O}$

Coefficients: $1 + 5 + 8 + 1 + 5 + 4 = 24$.

distractor_notes.A: 16 leaves out the $\ce{H+}$ needed to balance oxygen as water.
distractor_notes.B: 20 results from using $4\ce{H+}$ and $2\ce{H2O}$, which does not balance O.
distractor_notes.D: 28 double-counts the water or uses 6 Fe instead of 5.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
The half-cell with the more positive $E^\circ$ is the cathode (reduction): $\ce{Ag+ + e- -> Ag}$.

$E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode} = 0.80 - (-0.76) = +1.56\ \text{V}$.

Multiplying the Ag half-reaction by 2 to balance electrons does not change its potential.

distractor_notes.B: 0.04 V comes from computing $0.80 - 0.76$, dropping the sign of the Zn potential.
distractor_notes.C: 2.36 V doubles the Ag potential when balancing electrons; potentials are intensive and are not multiplied.
distractor_notes.D: A negative $E^\circ_\text{cell}$ would mean the reaction is not spontaneous as written, but a galvanic cell runs spontaneously.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
In a galvanic cell, oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

Electrons leave the anode through the external wire, so the anode is negative and the cathode positive.

The salt bridge carries ions, not electrons: cations move toward the cathode (where positive charge is being consumed) and anions move toward the anode (where positive charge is being produced).

distractor_notes.A: Oxidation is always at the anode; reduction at the cathode (in both galvanic and electrolytic cells).
distractor_notes.B: Electrons move through the external wire; only ions move through the salt bridge.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: anions flow toward the anode to neutralize the metal cations produced there.
distractor_notes.D: In a galvanic cell the cathode is positive; it is negative only in an electrolytic cell.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Charge: $q = It = (2.00\ \text{A})(965\ \text{s}) = 1930\ \text{C}$.

Moles of electrons: $1930 / 96485 = 0.0200\ \text{mol e}^-$.

$\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$, so mol Cu $= 0.0100$ mol.

Mass $= 0.0100 \times 63.55 = 0.636\ \text{g}$.

distractor_notes.A: 1.27 g assumes one electron per Cu; $\ce{Cu^2+}$ needs two.
distractor_notes.B: 0.318 g uses four electrons per Cu.
distractor_notes.C: 2.54 g uses one electron per Cu and also doubles the charge.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: 0.0200 mol e⁻ → 0.0100 mol Cu → 0.636 g.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Overall: $\ce{Zn + Cu^2+ -> Zn^2+ + Cu}$, $n = 2$, $Q = [\ce{Zn^2+}]/[\ce{Cu^2+}] = 0.010$.

Nernst: $E = E^\circ - \dfrac{0.0592}{n}\log Q = 1.10 - \dfrac{0.0592}{2}(-2) = 1.10 + 0.0592 = 1.16\ \text{V}$.

A low product-ion concentration pushes the reaction forward, raising $E$ above $E^\circ$.

distractor_notes.A: 1.04 V has the sign of the correction reversed ($\log Q$ is negative here).
distractor_notes.B: 1.10 V is $E^\circ$; concentrations are not standard, so $E \ne E^\circ$.
distractor_notes.D: 1.22 V uses $n = 1$ instead of $n = 2$.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Potentials are not additive, but $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$ is.

$\ce{Fe^3+ + e- -> Fe^2+}$: $\Delta G^\circ = -1F(0.77)$

$\ce{Fe^2+ + 2e- -> Fe}$: $\Delta G^\circ = -2F(-0.44)$

Sum: $\Delta G^\circ = -F(0.77 - 0.88) = +0.11F$ for the 3-electron process, so $E^\circ = -0.11/3 = -0.037\ \text{V} \approx -0.04\ \text{V}$.

distractor_notes.B: +0.33 V simply adds the two potentials; potentials are intensive and cannot be added for a combined half-reaction.
distractor_notes.C: +0.165 V is the unweighted average; the weighting must be by electrons transferred.
distractor_notes.D: −0.11 V is the electron-weighted sum before dividing by $n = 3$.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.80 - 0.34 = 0.46\ \text{V}$; $n = 2$ electrons are transferred (two $\ce{Ag+}$ reduced per Cu).

$\log K = \dfrac{nE^\circ}{0.0592} = \dfrac{2(0.46)}{0.0592} = 15.5$

$K = 10^{15.5} \approx 3 \times 10^{15}$.

distractor_notes.A: $6 \times 10^7$ uses $n = 1$.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: $\log K = 15.5$.
distractor_notes.C: $3 \times 10^{38}$ adds the two potentials ($1.14$ V) instead of subtracting.
distractor_notes.D: $1 \times 10^{31}$ uses $n = 4$ (counting electrons in both half-reactions separately).

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$l$ can take integer values from $0$ to $n - 1$, and $m_l$ from $-l$ to $+l$.

For $n = 3$, $l$ can be 0, 1, or 2 only. $l = 3$ would describe an f subshell, which does not exist in the third shell.

distractor_notes.A: $(3,2,-2)$ is a 3d orbital; allowed.
distractor_notes.B: $(2,0,0)$ is the 2s orbital; allowed.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: $l = 3$ requires $n \ge 4$.
distractor_notes.D: $(4,1,-1)$ is a 4p orbital; allowed.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Argon accounts for 18 electrons; six remain.

The aufbau prediction is $4s^2 3d^4$, but chromium is an exception: a half-filled d subshell with all six electrons unpaired is lower in energy, giving $4s^1 3d^5$.

Copper ($4s^1 3d^{10}$) is the other common exception in this period.

distractor_notes.A: This is the naive aufbau result; Cr prefers the half-filled 3d.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: $4s^1 3d^5$, six unpaired electrons.
distractor_notes.C: That is seven valence electrons: manganese ($Z = 25$), not chromium.
distractor_notes.D: Placing all six electrons in 3d ignores that 4s is occupied in neutral atoms.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
All four species are isoelectronic (18 electrons).

With the same number of electrons, the nucleus with the fewest protons pulls least strongly: S (16) < Cl (17) < Ar (18) < K (19).

So the radius decreases $\ce{S^2-} > \ce{Cl-} > \ce{Ar} > \ce{K+}$.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: lowest nuclear charge in the isoelectronic series.
distractor_notes.B: $\ce{Cl-}$ is large but has one more proton than $\ce{S^2-}$.
distractor_notes.C: Neutral argon has 18 protons pulling the same 18 electrons.
distractor_notes.D: $\ce{K+}$ has the most protons and is the smallest.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
The general trend is increasing first ionization energy across a period, but there are two dips.

Be → B: the electron removed from B is in 2p, higher in energy than Be's 2s.

N → O: nitrogen has a half-filled 2p ($2p^3$); oxygen's fourth 2p electron is paired, and electron–electron repulsion makes it easier to remove. So $\text{IE}_1(\ce{O}) < \text{IE}_1(\ce{N})$.

distractor_notes.A: Be > Li: Be's 2s electrons are held more tightly by the higher nuclear charge; normal trend.
distractor_notes.B: C > B: both remove a 2p electron; normal trend. The dip is between Be and B, not B and C.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: pairing in oxygen's 2p makes it easier to ionize than nitrogen.
distractor_notes.D: Ne > F: normal trend; noble gases have the highest IE in their period.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\Delta E = 13.6\left(\dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{3^2}\right) = 13.6 \times \dfrac{5}{36} = 1.89\ \text{eV}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{1240}{1.89} = 656\ \text{nm}$

This is the red H-α line of the Balmer series.

distractor_notes.A: 122 nm is the Lyman-α line ($n = 2 \to 1$).
distractor_notes.B: 486 nm is $n = 4 \to 2$ (H-β).
distractor_notes.C: 1875 nm is $n = 4 \to 3$ (Paschen series).
distractor_notes.D: Correct: 1.89 eV corresponds to 656 nm.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Each PES peak corresponds to one subshell; peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in it.

2 : 2 : 6 : 2 → $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2$, a total of 12 electrons.

$Z = 12$ is magnesium.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2$ is Mg.
distractor_notes.B: Na would end 2 : 2 : 6 : 1 ($3s^1$).
distractor_notes.C: Ne has only three peaks (2 : 2 : 6).
distractor_notes.D: Al would show five peaks, ending with a $3p^1$ peak of height 1.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Alpha decay: mass number −4, atomic number −2 → $\ce{^{234}_{90}Th}$.

First β⁻: atomic number +1, mass unchanged → $\ce{^{234}_{91}Pa}$.

Second β⁻: → $\ce{^{234}_{92}U}$.

The net result is an isotope of the original element with mass number 4 lower.

distractor_notes.A: $\ce{^{234}Th}$ is the product after the alpha decay only.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: two β⁻ decays return $Z$ to 92.
distractor_notes.C: $\ce{^{230}Th}$ would require a second alpha decay.
distractor_notes.D: The alpha decay lowers $Z$ by 2 before the two β⁻ raise it by 2, and the mass number cannot stay 238.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\ce{Li^2+}$ has one electron and $Z = 3$.

$E_1 = -13.6 \times 3^2 / 1^2 = -122.4\ \text{eV}$.

Ionization energy is the energy to reach $n = \infty$ ($E = 0$): $122\ \text{eV}$, nine times that of hydrogen.

distractor_notes.A: 13.6 eV is hydrogen ($Z = 1$).
distractor_notes.B: 40.8 eV scales by $Z$ instead of $Z^2$.
distractor_notes.C: 367 eV scales by $Z^3$.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: $13.6 \times 9 = 122$ eV.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Sulfur has 6 valence electrons; four bond to F, leaving one lone pair.

Five electron domains → trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry.

The lone pair occupies an equatorial position (fewer 90° repulsions), giving a seesaw molecular shape.

distractor_notes.A: Tetrahedral ignores the lone pair on S.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: 4 bonds + 1 lone pair = seesaw.
distractor_notes.C: Square planar needs 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs (e.g., $\ce{XeF4}$).
distractor_notes.D: Trigonal pyramidal is 3 bonds + 1 lone pair (e.g., $\ce{NH3}$).

author: claude-seed

body_md:
A molecule is nonpolar when its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry.

$\ce{XeF4}$ is square planar (two lone pairs opposite each other), so the four Xe–F dipoles cancel.

$\ce{SF4}$ (seesaw), $\ce{PCl3}$ (trigonal pyramidal) and $\ce{SO2}$ (bent) all have lone pairs that break the symmetry.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: square planar, dipoles cancel.
distractor_notes.B: Seesaw shape; net dipole.
distractor_notes.C: Trigonal pyramidal; net dipole along the lone-pair axis.
distractor_notes.D: Bent; net dipole.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Cl has 7 valence electrons: three are used in Cl–F bonds, leaving two lone pairs.

Electron domains: 3 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 5 → trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry → $sp^3d$ hybridization.

The molecular shape is T-shaped, with both lone pairs equatorial.

distractor_notes.A: $sp^2$ is three domains.
distractor_notes.B: $sp^3$ is four domains; that would be $\ce{NF3}$-like.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: five electron domains.
distractor_notes.D: $sp^3d^2$ is six domains (e.g., $\ce{BrF5}$).

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\ce{O2}$ has 12 valence electrons: $(\sigma_{2s})^2(\sigma^*_{2s})^2(\sigma_{2p})^2(\pi_{2p})^4(\pi^*_{2p})^2$, bond order $(8-4)/2 = 2$.

$\ce{O2-}$ adds one electron to a $\pi^*$ orbital: bonding 8, antibonding 5.

Bond order $= (8 - 5)/2 = 1.5$.

distractor_notes.A: 1 is the peroxide ion, $\ce{O2^2-}$.
distractor_notes.C: 2 is neutral $\ce{O2}$.
distractor_notes.D: 2.5 is $\ce{O2+}$ (an electron removed from $\pi^*$).

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Formal charge $=$ valence electrons $-$ nonbonding electrons $- \tfrac{1}{2}$(bonding electrons).

In both major resonance forms the central N has four bonds and no lone pairs: $\ce{N#N-O}$ and $\ce{N=N=O}$.

FC(central N) $= 5 - 0 - 4 = +1$ in each. The −1 charge sits on O (preferred, more electronegative) or on the terminal N.

distractor_notes.A: −1 is the formal charge on O in the $\ce{N#N-O}$ structure.
distractor_notes.B: FC = 0 would need one lone pair and three bonds on the central N, which cannot complete the octets of both neighbors.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: four bonds and no lone pairs gives +1.
distractor_notes.D: +2 would require five bonds, impossible for nitrogen.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Lone pairs compress bond angles: $\ce{CH4}$ (109.5°) > $\ce{NH3}$ (107°) > $\ce{H2O}$ (104.5°).

Going down a group, the central atom is larger and less electronegative; the bonding pairs sit farther from it and repel each other less, and the bonds use nearly pure p orbitals.

$\ce{H2S}$ has a bond angle of about 92°, the smallest of the four.

distractor_notes.A: No lone pairs; ideal tetrahedral angle.
distractor_notes.B: One lone pair; 107°.
distractor_notes.C: Two lone pairs; 104.5°, but S is larger than O.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: two lone pairs on a larger central atom; ~92°.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Bond length decreases as bond order increases.

MO bond orders: $\ce{O2+}$ 2.5, $\ce{O2}$ 2, $\ce{O2-}$ 1.5, $\ce{O2^2-}$ 1.

Removing an electron from an antibonding $\pi^*$ orbital strengthens and shortens the bond, so $\ce{O2+}$ has the shortest bond (~112 pm).

distractor_notes.A: Bond order 2; second shortest.
distractor_notes.B: Bond order 1.5.
distractor_notes.C: Bond order 1; the longest.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: highest bond order, 2.5.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Count unpaired electrons using the MO diagram (for $\ce{B2}$–$\ce{N2}$, $\pi_{2p}$ lies below $\sigma_{2p}$).

$\ce{B2}$: 6 valence e⁻, $(\pi_{2p})^2$ with one electron in each degenerate π orbital → 2 unpaired, paramagnetic.

$\ce{C2}$: $(\pi_{2p})^4$ → all paired. $\ce{N2}$: all paired.

$\ce{O2}$: $(\pi^*_{2p})^2$ → 2 unpaired. $\ce{NO}$: 11 valence e⁻, $(\pi^*)^1$ → 1 unpaired.

Paramagnetic: $\ce{B2}$, $\ce{O2}$, $\ce{NO}$ = 3.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: $\ce{B2}$, $\ce{O2}$ and $\ce{NO}$.
distractor_notes.B: Counting only $\ce{O2}$ misses $\ce{B2}$ (Hund's rule in $\pi_{2p}$) and $\ce{NO}$ (odd electron).
distractor_notes.C: $\ce{O2}$ and $\ce{NO}$ alone misses $\ce{B2}$.
distractor_notes.D: $\ce{C2}$ is diamagnetic: its four π electrons fill both $\pi_{2p}$ orbitals.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Flame colors arise from electrons in the metal ion relaxing after thermal excitation.

Common results: $\ce{Na+}$ intense yellow, $\ce{K+}$ lilac, $\ce{Li+}$ crimson, $\ce{Sr^2+}$ red, $\ce{Ca^2+}$ brick red/orange, $\ce{Ba^2+}$ apple green, $\ce{Cu^2+}$ blue-green.

Apple green points to barium.

distractor_notes.A: Sodium is bright yellow.
distractor_notes.B: Potassium is lilac (often masked by sodium).
distractor_notes.C: Strontium is crimson red.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: barium gives apple green.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Color in aqueous transition-metal ions comes from d–d transitions, which require a partially filled d subshell.

$\ce{Zn^2+}$ is $d^{10}$ (completely filled), so no d–d transition is possible and its solutions are colorless.

$\ce{Cu^2+}$ ($d^9$) is blue, $\ce{Ni^2+}$ ($d^8$) green, $\ce{Fe^3+}$ ($d^5$) yellow-brown.

distractor_notes.A: Blue.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: $d^{10}$, colorless.
distractor_notes.C: Green.
distractor_notes.D: Yellow to brown.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Check each possible product against the solubility rules.

$\ce{Pb^2+ + 2I- -> PbI2(s)}$: lead(II) iodide is insoluble and precipitates as a bright yellow solid.

All nitrates, and the chlorides of Na, K and Ba, are soluble; $\ce{NH4Cl + NaOH}$ releases $\ce{NH3}$ gas on warming but forms no solid.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: yellow $\ce{PbI2}$.
distractor_notes.B: All possible products are soluble alkali-metal salts.
distractor_notes.C: Produces $\ce{NH3(g)}$ and water, not a solid.
distractor_notes.D: $\ce{BaCl2}$ is soluble (barium sulfate is the insoluble one).

author: claude-seed

body_md: Standard gas tests: $\ce{O2}$ relights a glowing splint; $\ce{H2}$ gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint; $\ce{CO2}$ turns limewater milky and extinguishes a flame; $\ce{N2}$ is inert and extinguishes a flame.

distractor_notes.A: Hydrogen burns with a pop but does not relight a glowing splint.
distractor_notes.B: Carbon dioxide extinguishes flames.
distractor_notes.C: Nitrogen extinguishes flames.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: oxygen supports combustion.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
A buret is calibrated to deliver any volume up to its capacity, read to ±0.01–0.05 mL, which is why it is used in titrations.

A volumetric pipet delivers one fixed volume; a volumetric flask contains (does not deliver) one fixed volume; a graduated cylinder is only approximate.

distractor_notes.A: Contains a single fixed volume; used for making solutions.
distractor_notes.B: Variable but low precision.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: precise and variable.
distractor_notes.D: Precise but a single fixed volume.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Amphoteric hydroxides react with both acids and strong bases.

$\ce{Zn(OH)2(s) + 2OH- -> [Zn(OH)4]^2-(aq)}$ (tetrahydroxozincate), so the white precipitate redissolves in excess base.

$\ce{Al(OH)3}$, $\ce{Pb(OH)2}$, $\ce{Sn(OH)2}$ and $\ce{Cr(OH)3}$ behave similarly. $\ce{Mg(OH)2}$ and $\ce{Fe(OH)3}$ are purely basic and stay as precipitates.

distractor_notes.A: Basic only; remains insoluble in excess base.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: amphoteric, forms $\ce{[Zn(OH)4]^2-}$.
distractor_notes.C: The rust-brown precipitate is not amphoteric.
distractor_notes.D: Not amphoteric; sparingly soluble regardless of excess base.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Ionic hydrides contain the hydride ion, $\ce{H-}$, a strong base and reducing agent.

$\ce{NaH + H2O -> NaOH + H2}$: the hydride is oxidized to $\ce{H2}$ and the solution is strongly basic.

$\ce{CaO}$ gives $\ce{Ca(OH)2}$ (basic, but no gas); $\ce{NH3}$ gives a weakly basic solution, no gas; $\ce{SO2}$ gives acidic sulfurous acid.

distractor_notes.A: Basic solution but no hydrogen evolved.
distractor_notes.B: Weak base; no redox, no gas.
distractor_notes.C: Acidic oxide.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: hydride reduces water to $\ce{H2}$, leaving $\ce{OH-}$.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
No precipitate with $\ce{Cl-}$ rules out $\ce{Ag+}$ (white $\ce{AgCl}$).

A white precipitate with sulfate points to $\ce{BaSO4}$, one of the least soluble sulfates. $\ce{CuSO4}$ and $\ce{Na2SO4}$ are soluble (and a $\ce{Cu^2+}$ solution would be blue).

The ion is $\ce{Ba^2+}$.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: soluble chloride, insoluble white sulfate.
distractor_notes.B: Would have precipitated white $\ce{AgCl}$ with HCl.
distractor_notes.C: Copper sulfate is soluble; the solution would also be blue.
distractor_notes.D: All common sodium salts are soluble.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Find the longest chain containing the –OH carbon: four carbons (butanol).

Number from the end nearest the –OH group: C1 bears the OH, so the methyl branch is on C3.

Name: 3-methylbutan-1-ol (also written 3-methyl-1-butanol).

distractor_notes.A: 2-methylbutan-1-ol is $\ce{CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2OH}$, a different isomer.
distractor_notes.B: Numbering from the wrong end gives locant 4 for OH; the OH must get the lowest number.
distractor_notes.C: Correct.
distractor_notes.D: A 4-methylbutane is really a five-carbon chain (pentane).

author: claude-seed

body_md:
The fragment $\ce{-C(=O)-O-C}$ is an ester: a carbonyl carbon bonded to an alkoxy group.

$\ce{CH3COOCH2CH3}$ is ethyl acetate (ethyl ethanoate), made from acetic acid and ethanol.

An ether has $\ce{C-O-C}$ with no carbonyl; a carboxylic acid ends in $\ce{-COOH}$.

distractor_notes.A: Ethers lack the C=O.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: ethyl ethanoate.
distractor_notes.C: A ketone's carbonyl is bonded to two carbons, not to an oxygen.
distractor_notes.D: The acidic H has been replaced by an ethyl group.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Start from the two butane skeletons.

n-butane: Cl on C1 (1-chlorobutane) or C2 (2-chlorobutane).

2-methylpropane: Cl on a terminal carbon (1-chloro-2-methylpropane) or the central carbon (2-chloro-2-methylpropane).

Total: 4 constitutional isomers. (2-chlorobutane is also chiral, but stereoisomers are not counted here.)

distractor_notes.A: Correct: 2 from butane + 2 from 2-methylpropane.
distractor_notes.B: Counts only the straight-chain isomers.
distractor_notes.C: Misses one position on the branched skeleton.
distractor_notes.D: Counting the enantiomers of 2-chlorobutane separately gives 5 stereoisomers, but only 4 constitutional isomers.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Geometric isomerism requires a C=C double bond with two different groups on each alkene carbon.

But-2-ene: each alkene carbon has H and $\ce{CH3}$ → cis and trans forms exist.

But-1-ene has two H's on C1; 2-methylpropene has two $\ce{CH3}$ groups on the same carbon; an alkyne is linear and has no geometric isomers.

distractor_notes.A: The terminal $\ce{=CH2}$ carbon has two identical substituents.
distractor_notes.B: $\ce{(CH3)2C=CH2}$: identical groups on each carbon.
distractor_notes.C: Triple bonds are linear; no cis/trans.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH3}$.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
The π bond of the alkene is broken and two new σ bonds form; all atoms of both reactants end up in the single product.

That is an addition reaction (specifically electrophilic addition of bromine). The rapid loss of bromine's color is a classic test for unsaturation.

distractor_notes.A: Substitution swaps one group for another (e.g., alkane + $\ce{Br2}$ under UV light).
distractor_notes.B: Elimination is the reverse: removing atoms to form a double bond.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: everything adds across the double bond.
distractor_notes.D: Condensation joins two molecules with loss of a small molecule such as water.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
There are two stereocenters (C2 and C3), so the maximum is $2^2 = 4$.

But the molecule is symmetric: the (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) forms are the same compound, a meso isomer with an internal mirror plane.

Stereoisomers: the meso compound plus the (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair of enantiomers = 3.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: one meso form + one enantiomeric pair.
distractor_notes.B: Two would be a single enantiomeric pair; the meso form is a separate compound.
distractor_notes.C: $2^n$ overcounts when a meso form exists.
distractor_notes.D: Six is not possible for two stereocenters.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Compare conjugate-base stability.

Carboxylic acids beat phenol and alcohols because the carboxylate charge is delocalized over two oxygens.

Among carboxylic acids, an electron-withdrawing chlorine on the α-carbon stabilizes the anion further by induction: chloroacetic acid ($\text{p}K_a \approx 2.9$) is stronger than acetic acid ($\text{p}K_a \approx 4.8$).

distractor_notes.A: Acetic acid lacks the inductive stabilization of chloroacetic acid.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: the inductive effect of Cl lowers the p$K_a$.
distractor_notes.C: Ethanol, p$K_a$ ≈ 16, is barely acidic.
distractor_notes.D: Phenol (p$K_a$ ≈ 10) is more acidic than alcohols but much weaker than carboxylic acids.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Tollens' reagent, $\ce{[Ag(NH3)2]+}$, oxidizes aldehydes to carboxylates while depositing silver metal; ketones, ethers and alcohols do not react.

Of the $\ce{C4H8O}$ candidates, only butanal, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CHO}$, is an aldehyde.

All four are isomers: the one degree of unsaturation appears as a C=O, a ring, or a C=C.

distractor_notes.A: A ketone; not oxidized by Tollens'.
distractor_notes.B: A cyclic ether; unreactive.
distractor_notes.C: An alkene alcohol; alcohols are not oxidized by Tollens'.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: the aldehyde.
